title: AI Automation Cost in 2026: What You Pay for Build, Runtime, and Upkeep
excerpt: AI automation costs €5,000 to €40,000 to build and €50 to €800 a month to run in 2026. Here is the full price breakdown by use case, the five factors that move a quote, and how to scope a first build that pays back in weeks.
metaDescription: What does AI automation cost? Real 2026 ranges by use case, the costs no one quotes, and how to scope a first build that pays back fast.

blocks.text: AI automation cost in 2026 breaks into three lines: a **€5,000 to €40,000 build**, **€50 to €800 a month** to run it, and a maintenance budget most quotes never show you. A single workflow sits near the floor. A company-wide agent stack sits at the ceiling.
Two companies ask for the same invoice automation and get quotes €25,000 apart. The gap comes from how many systems the automation touches and how expensive a wrong output is.

You have probably seen estimates swing from a few thousand to six figures and wondered which one is honest. This guide prices each line of an AI automation: build, runtime, and upkeep. You get real 2026 ranges by use case, the five factors that move a quote, and a way to scope a first build that pays back fast.

items: **A single AI automation runs €5,000 to €15,000 to build** and €50 to €800 a month to run. Multi-system builds reach €40,000 and beyond.
**Build is the cheap part.** Maintenance, integrations, and edge cases decide the real three-year cost.
**Five factors move every quote:** integration count, data quality, review and audit requirements, volume and model choice, and failure handling.
**No-code stacks look cheaper in euros** while burying the cost in fragile team hours and platform fees that pass €1,700 a year.
**Scope the task that wastes the most hours first.** A workflow that runs 50-plus times a month pays back in weeks.

blocks.text: The three layers of AI automation cost
Every AI automation bills across three layers. You pay once to build it, then every month to run it and keep it alive. Most quotes show the first layer clearly and stay vague on the other two.

The build is the engineering: wiring the automation into your tools, writing the logic, adding review steps, and shipping it to production. webvise scopes [AI workflow automation](/services/ai-automation) as a fixed build price after a short discovery call, with a 3 to 6 week timeline for a first workflow.
Runtime is what the automation spends while it works: model API calls and hosting. A light classification job costs €50 a month. A high-volume document agent on a frontier model can pass €800.

Maintenance keeps it working when an API key rotates, a model price changes, or a source system updates. webvise runs this as a €200 to €800 monthly retainer so the fixing time stays off your team's plate.

blocks.text: What AI automation costs by use case
The fastest way to estimate your own cost is to find the workflow closest to yours. The ranges below come from real 2026 builds across document generation, data sync, support, and reporting.

Document and proposal generation sits at the top of the single-workflow bracket whenever brand voice and exact formatting matter. A documentary producer who pitches commissions to broadcasters had us build a writing pipeline in 2026 that turns an idea into a broadcaster-ready document in under three hours, in his own voice, with every claim traced to a source.

That build took two weeks and cost more than a plain data sync for one reason. The output had to match a voice corpus drawn from eight past pitches and render with deterministic typography, so one off-tone page could not lose a six-figure commission. Voice fidelity and exact formatting pushed it into the upper bracket.

The five factors that move a quote
Two builds in the same use-case row can still differ by €20,000. Five factors explain almost all of that spread.

items: **Integration count and type.** A webhook into one SaaS app is cheap. Direct wiring into a CRM, an ERP, and a database with two-way sync is where the hours go.
**Data quality.** Clean, structured inputs keep the build short. Messy PDFs, scanned forms, and inconsistent naming add extraction and cleanup work before the automation runs at all.
**Review and audit requirements.** A workflow that writes to production needs human-in-the-loop steps, approval states, and an audit trail. Those guardrails are engineering, and they cost.
**Volume and model choice.** A frontier model on 40,000 runs a month costs far more at runtime than a small model on 500. The right model is a budget decision made during scoping.

**Failure handling.** Programmatic retries, alerting, and fallbacks separate an automation that survives a bad night from one that silently drops work. Skipping them is cheap upfront and expensive later.

blocks.text: The costs no one quotes
The build line is visible. The recurring drift underneath it is the part teams underestimate, and it is where automations quietly get expensive.

Models change prices and get deprecated. API keys rotate. A source system ships an update that breaks a parser at 2 a.m. Someone has to own the fix, and when that someone is an internal engineer, the real cost is their time, not a line on an invoice.

No-code stacks hide the same cost in plain sight. A team running Zapier plus Make plus a half-finished n8n instance pays roughly €1,700 a year in platform fees before any useful work happens, then spends hours every month replaying failed runs across two dashboards. We broke that math down in [n8n vs Make vs Zapier](/blog/n8n-vs-make-vs-zapier-2026).
This is why webvise prices maintenance as a flat retainer. The fixing time becomes predictable and stays off your team's calendar.
No-code versus custom: the three-year cost
Over a single month, a no-code automation almost always looks cheaper. Over three years the comparison changes, because the cheap option spends your team's hours instead of your budget.

blocks.text: The custom build costs more cash and far fewer hours, and it keeps working when volume grows. The no-code stack wins on a tight first-year budget and on workflows you expect to stay small. We walk through that decision in [build versus buy software](/blog/build-vs-buy-software-2026).
How to scope a first automation that pays back
You control most of the cost at the scoping stage, before anyone writes code. Four rules keep a first build cheap and fast to payback.

items: **Start with the task your team complains about most.** It is usually document processing, report generation, or moving data between two systems. The loudest complaint is also the highest-hours workflow.
**Set a volume floor.** A workflow that runs at least 50 times a month is worth automating. Below that, the build rarely earns back its cost.
**Ask for a fixed build price after discovery.** A short discovery call should produce a scoped estimate, a timeline, and a clear runtime budget before you commit a euro.
**Put monitoring and fallbacks in scope from day one.** An automation you cannot see is an automation you cannot trust. The dashboard is part of the build, not an upsell.
